method: A printed map draws one millimetre of paper as the scale denominator in millimetres of ground, so a sheet's ground coverage is its printable width and height (trimmed paper minus twice the margin) divided by 1,000 and multiplied by the scale denominator. The page lays that coverage in a rectangular grid and counts sheets by ceil((target - overlap) / (coverage - overlap)) on each axis, where the overlap is the paper overlap times the scale; the overlap appears on both sides of the division because every sheet after the first reuses one overlap strip, so overlap reduces the ground each extra sheet adds rather than the sheet's own coverage. A target that exactly fills the last sheet keeps that count and any part beyond it adds one. The grid extent is sheets x coverage minus (sheets - 1) overlaps, and the paper area is the sheet count times the untrimmed paper area. The same paper, margins and overlap are then reapplied at 1:10,000, 1:25,000, 1:50,000, 1:100,000, 1:250,000 and 1:500,000 to show the sheet count at other common scales. The model assumes one uniform map scale over the whole area, a rectangular grid with straight joins, uniform margins and that the entered margin is printable; it ignores projection distortion away from a map's standard parallel or central meridian, a printer's own unprintable edge, trimming and folding, and it treats the area as a rectangle rather than a shaped region. Inputs are 0.01 to 5,000 km per side, a whole scale denominator from 1,000 to 1,000,000, margins and overlaps from 0 to 100 mm with the printable size kept positive and the overlap smaller than it; there is no storage, upload or network access.
